This is a great game and in time will only get better. Once you learn how to play it draws you deep into its creative ASCII world. There is a lot to do but the game is mostly about managing your kingdom and attacking hostile factions. Most recently the diplomacy system and combat has been re-worked and has much improved over earlier versions. After well into 70 turns into the game I was able to convince an ally to become a Vassal of my Empire. Pretty darn cool!

If you didn't grow up in the 80s or 90's this game may be a tough sell because of how it looks. But don't let its looks fool you, once it harnesses your imagination you will lose many hours playing this. While Steam only shows 8.8 hours of play time my actual time is closer to 30 hours. During an update it corrupted my save files, so I create a manual backup of the game after every session and launch the copy outside of steam. Which is easy to do since the game engine is really just C++ code that manipulates the command console. As for the nostalgia factor the game scores very high for me, since is reminds me of the early Q-basic games I played as kid.

The developer is really friendly and eager to support community suggestions and ideas on how to improve the game. While many elements of the  game still could use polish, the limits of using the command console restrict much of what can be done. But clever design can certainly work around those limitations.

However as it stands Warsim is a charming Beer & Pretzels type of game that is low stress but still challenging and engaging to those with a fair amount of time and imagination.

From the outside, VVVVVV may just look like another retro-styled game that uses its retro factor to hide the fact that it's just another generic platformer. While the former may be true, this is definitely not your average platformer.

The story of this game is simple: you're a captain of a spaceship and your crew has been scattered through another dimension due to some interference. You need to find them and stop the interference. The graphic style is heavily inspired by the Commodore 64's graphics, while the sountrack is more reminiscent of that of the NES. Both of these work great together, although they might not be amusing for someone is tired of retro styled indie games.

VVVVVV is a metroidvania game: meaning that you can explore the dimension you're in looking for all sorts of things (crew members, trinkets, teleporters). What makes VVVVVV so special however is that you can't jump, but you can flip gravity so that you'll go up instead of down, and vice-versa. The concept is easy to learn (but incredibly hard to master), and leads to many creative levels. There will be some levels [spoiler]*cough*Doing Things The Hard Way*cough*[/spoiler] that will usually frustrate the crap out of you, but at the same time you'll have a blast trying to figure out how to get through them (unless you are [b]very[/b] easily frustrated, in which case, you should stay away from this game). On top of the main game, there are tons of other features that will keep you playing for hours, such as collecting all of the trinkets, time trials, various game modes ([b]flip mode[/b] where the entire game is flipped upside down and [b]no death mode[/b] where if you die once you have to restart the game), and even a level creator.


VVVVVV will make you want to break your keyboard and you will love every minute of it. What makes this game even better is that it's often on sale for a low price (sometimes even $0.49!). This is a must have for those looking for a challenge.

After 14 hours and finishing this game. I can say it sucks. Redfail is a hot pot of half baked ideas, that are thrown together and nothing works. It's almost like Arkane threw darts at a idea board and said yea that will work.

::Initial Thoughts::
My opening impressions of the game before playing were the teaser and the controversial gameplay showcase, and neither impressed me. But as a passionate fan of Arkane, I bought the game on release anyway. And to my relief, it was better than I had been led to believe. I would like to point out that I have only played the game single-player so far, and that’s the perspective I am using in this review.

::Gameplay and Story::
- The vampires in this game give it a surreal, campy, and semi-spooky atmosphere, not unlike Buffy or an 80's horror. Every nook and crawlspace has the environmental storytelling that Arkane's known for, making it fun to explore even the most unassuming tool shed or bathroom. Overall the town feels well crafted and (recently) alive, like it’s worth fighting for.
- The gunplay feels weighty and responsive and the fights feel satisfying - when approached correctly. There’s a Borderlands vibe with the gun collection and sorting, making the looter-shooter label fairly accurate.
- The powers are visually interesting while adding an entertaining depth to the combat and world navigation. While it is fun playing alone, there’s the sinking feeling that the powers could be used even more efficiently and creatively together with other players.
- The story is just fine so far. There’s a high air of charisma from the player-characters that contrast quite well with the "quietly surviving" tone of the NPC's as you assist them. There's an overarching story that unfolds as you progress, but as I haven’t finished the game, I don’t know where it’s leading. Overall there’s nothing trailblazing from the story, but it seems perfectly suited for a game of killing vampires and soaking in atmosphere.

::Thoughts on Multiplayer::
Marketing for this game enthusiastically promoted this as a multiplayer game. I was concerned there’d be a hollow feeling as I played the game alone. As if the game would always pressure me to invite friends or frequently promote co-op only features. This was NOT the case, and the choice seems to lie solely on the player’s preference.

::Critiques::
- When you're not fighting something spooky, you're fighting a human cult/gang member. I figure this was for variety’s sake, to not overuse the beastly things and have them lose their sense of suspense. But they certainly are less interesting, and it feels like you fight them more than vampires.
- The default ADS is not 1:1. It's much lower than the mouse sensitivity making it quite cumbersome to counteract. As of now there is no option to adjust this.
- The overall game difficulty is relatively low. I'm playing it on 3/4 difficulty just to feel threatened. I'd probably insist on playing it on 4/4 difficulty if I were playing with friends. But to play on 4/4, you first need to beat the game on any other difficulty. If I wasn’t planning to play solo my first run anyway, I could see this being frustrating.

::Final Thoughts::
- When first starting the game, I picked the author, but didn't really vibe with it. So I started over as the psychic college student and enjoyed it more. This just to say, you might want to try out a character or two before settling in for a playthrough.
- I haven't read any of the other reviews yet as I wanted my first impression to be formed in a vacuum. But I do know the price is kinda steep and the reviews don't seem very positive right now. If that worries you, you'd probably only regret your purchase. Better wait for everything to cool off or wait for the eventual sale.

Wasteland has always had a very unique flare to its games. Wasteland 3 is certainly unique, but it is also very disappointing in comparison to Wasteland 2. 

I'm going to do this in a bullet point form to make this simple:

Pros
-Story is great, although there is a lot of boring dialogue that I eventually found myself skipping by. As with Wasteland 2, I eventually found myself just playing to kill stuff.
-Lots more customisation with outfits and character creation, although armour now shows on your character, so clothing is more or less irrelevant as you never see it.
-They have a lot more weapon variety. E.g. automatic weapons includes automatic bullet and energy weapons, big guns includes spewers(flamethrower, cryothrower etc.) and machine guns.
-Perks and skills have been changed a little bit, a lot less perks but the skills feel more unique now.
-Map travel is lovely. You get a nice snow-plow-tank to drive around in and it just looks cool.
-Sound design is pretty good. Music is very well done.
-Quests have a suggested level on the quest page, which is useful to know what you should be doing next.

Cons
-Difficulty/balancing is all kinds of wack. If you thought W2's difficulty was ridiculous at times, this game just feels unreal. I played on the default difficulty(Wastelander) and at some point I had to drop it down to Tourist(lowest). Overkill(and a lot less fun), but in virtually all fights my characters were being kill in easily 1 or 2 turns, even my 'tanky' character, and enemies are bullet sponges. I dropped the difficulty, and enemies go down by over 200% health (one enemy went from 200~ to 60~). The health and damage values are just insane in this game, it feels like they took the wrong lessons from W2 on balancing.
-Related to the difficulty, there's a lot less tactical options in W3. W2 wasn't the deepest game but it had a lot more depth than W3. Every fight in W3(at wastelander or higher difficulty) just feels like a turn-wide DPS check.
-Status effects are weird. There's some new status effects of course, but they reworked DoT and it's awful. Admittedly I don't remember how much damage they did but in W3 they do % damage, and DoTs last a long time. Having the first aid kit, or alternatively a lot of stims(which is realistically impossible), is essential which is a bit unfortunate as an optional skill.
-There does seem to be some bugs and issues but they are negligible in my experience.
-They removed initiative and who goes first in combat(the first turn) is dependent on who starts the fight. This is a big reason as to why I think the fights in W3 are "DPS checks" because all of your units act at the same time, and vice versa.

Of anything I could say, my biggest issue is with the combat. I find it unfathomable as to why these turn-based 'tactical' rpgs always find it so difficult to balance their games effectively. Obviously play on the difficulty that suits you, but this game is insane with its damage and health values at, what I assume is, the normal and standard difficulty. I'm talking double your health, quadruple your damage. It was very odd trying to play this game and I was very excited to finally try it, but I was met with utter disappointment. W2 was *much* easier on the normal difficulty (while the harder difficulties were fittingly BS in some parts) and while I appreciate the greater focus on combat with W3, they really dropped the ball here. It feels like they tried to make it more varied and interested but they forgot to balance all the new mechanics, the tweaks, and just everything really. Also, trying to have every skill available to you is somehow harder in W3 and there's weirdly high skill checks in areas / quests that are low suggested level, so expect lots of missed checks. I can't explain that one, it just felt like odd design.

EDIT: Also, to add to the bugs point, one of the biggest issues I've been having quite a big into my playthrough is lag spikes. To compare to this game, I've been able to run games like Cyberpunk 2077, DOOM 2016, and other beefy *OPTIMISED* games that dwarf this game in requirements. After playing through the game along with the included DLCs here's my review:

The Good
- Immersive Storytelling: Wasteland 3 offers a richly woven narrative with impactful choices. Some are immediate some takes a while before it pays off. From faction politics to moral dilemmas, your decisions shapes the world, also it gives the game some replay value. On my playthrough I helped Saul with bringing his children back alive, there are a lot of points in the story where it can branch out to different outcome and I loved that.
- Customisable Team: The character creation and progression system is intricate, letting you customize your squad with unique perks, quirks, and abilities. Team synergy and specialization is a must to explore the world of Wasteland 3. 
- Turn based Combat: The combat is engaging and challenging, as it requires the smart use of cover, positioning, and skills. And with the DLCs there are special objectives that spices up the battles. The battle of Steeltown gives you the opportunity to clear the DLC with non-lethal approach or not, depending on your style. The Holy Detonation requires you to move from point A to point B while in battle to activate a terminal or kill an enemy standing in a platform.
- Humor and Tone: The game’s dark humor and satirical take on a post-apocalyptic America are entertaining It balances its grim setting with quirky dialogue, outrageous characters, and bizarre situations. Also I loved the fact that you do not have to be the good guy everytime, and the game gives you the options to do so.
- Steam Deck Opotimization: I played this game on the steam deck, and the performance is impressive. I was able to max out all settings. It drains the battery really fast if you just let it on uncapped frame rate so I had to cap it to 30 and it gives me around 5 hours per full charge.

The Bad
- The Inventory Management: Maybe this is due to the fact that I am playing on a controller and this game is a CRPG, the inventory management can sometimes feel cumbersome, especially when juggling to multiple party members' gear. I also have to manually compare the second weapon manually since, the compare feature only shows the first one, not sure if there is a button to press that I am not aware of.
- Pathfinding: There are times were some of the characters moves randomly than you expect them to move, resulting in one of them triggering landmines or tripwires that I was carefully avoiding. 
- Ending just ends: I was expecting a good climax like when some characters are introduced for the first time and it is on 1st person perspective. On my playthrough, at the very end, Saul just approached me and asked some questions and that's it, the screen turns black and someone starts singing about the epilogue then the credits rolled. 

The Ugly:
- Wasteland 3, although is a masterpiece, it isn't free from bugs, I experienced getting stucked before a cutscene and had to reload my most recent save. Also in combat, there are times where characters are getting stuck in tight spaces and just soft locks the combat. Pretty sure those issues won't be fixed as the last update was some years ago.
- The DLCs requires internet to be able to play and get recognized. I travel a lot and had to start wasteland 3 and load my latest save before I move away from the internet. This is minor but still annoying and I am pretty sure they could have easily fixed this but they didn't 

Final Thoughts:
Wasteland 3 is a fantastic mix of choice-driven storytelling and tactical combat, and playing it on the Steam Deck makes it even better with the added convenience of portability. Sure, it has a few rough edges and technical hiccups, but it’s still a must-play for RPG and CRPG fans who's into post-apocalyptic settings. I highly recommend this game

I highly recommend this game if you're looking for something that offers more than just gameplay. Tl;Dr - I enjoyed it. It's a pretty addictive tavern sim with satisfying progression and a great core gameplay loop, however, pricing of 'Games' (archery, strength test, punching bags, etc) is ridiculous and needs to be re-looked at.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Overview[/h2]
Tavern Master is a wonderful medieval tavern management simulator that lets you build and run your very own medieval tavern. You start off with simple wooden benches and a small bar with a keg of water, and slowly evolve into a multi-storey hub filled with laughter and food.

I’ve spent around 30 hours fine-tuning floor plans, decorating, and squeezing out every coin from satisfied patrons. It’s incredibly satisfying watching your little medieval empire grow from a humble beginning.

[h2]Gameplay & Progression[/h2]
At its core, it's quite an addictive blend of strategy, planning, and resource management. The gameplay is smooth and intuitive: build, decorate, hire, expand, repeat. The mechanics are well-balanced, but progression can sometimes feel like a slog. I'll be honest, I wasn't a fan at first, but the fire extinguisher mechanic is well-thought through.

One area that felt a bit lacklustre was the 'Games' section. These additions are nice in theory, adding an interactive element to entertain guests, but in practice, they feel more like an expensive luxury with little return. I found the pricing completely out of proportion to the benefit - often having just a 40% chance for a game to trigger a mere 10 gold charge (it costs 25k to set up). It’s hard to justify the cost when you're looking to optimise profit. Also, it takes up valuable table space when a patron will pay 50x more.

A final negative would be the level up system. Level ups feel nondescript and underwhelming, especially when speed is irrelevant on researchers.

[h2]Audio[/h2]
If there’s one area where Tavern Master didn’t quite hit the mark for me, it’s the music. The soundtrack felt repetitive and uninspired, which is a shame given how much time you’ll likely spend immersed in the game. In the end, I played with the music muted and opted for my own playlist instead. While it’s not a dealbreaker, a more dynamic or ambient score would have really helped elevate the atmosphere.

[h2]Visuals & Interface[/h2]
The game’s visual style is clean and appealing (although outside of the tavern doesn't look too great), with a vibrant, almost storybook aesthetic that suits the medieval theme perfectly. Watching guests come and go, servers dashing around with mugs of wine (yes... mugs of wine) and entertainers strumming lutes in the corner adds real character to the experience.

The UI is also well-designed and scaleable for your own preference, though it could benefit from a few quality-of-life tweaks here and there (such as more precise placement tools or batch upgrades for certain items). Still, it never got in the way of the fun.

[h2]Value for Money[/h2]
At its current price point, Tavern Master offers solid value. There’s plenty of content to keep you engaged for dozens of hours, and it’s the kind of game you’ll likely revisit from time to time just to try out new layouts or chase perfection (especially with the sandbox mode). I bought it on sale, but would say it's worth it.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
If you enjoy tycoon-style games or have ever dreamed of running your own medieval inn, Tavern Master will absolutely scratch that itch.

You have to make all kinds of decisions about whether you want to spend gold on your heroes by upgrading them or curing them of illness or getting rid of annoying quirks or whether you just want to dismiss them altogether to save yourself the hassle. You also get to decide what kind of build you want to have on your heroes and what kinds of comps you want to take into the differing dungeons. This game does a great job of providing a problem and giving you tons of ways to solve it and that freedom to choose is what makes the game so interesting and creates a great gameplay loop. I have over 200 hours in this game and I still haven't tried every build and every class in the game yet, I still haven't tried using certain trinkets and haven't finished the DLCs but I always get super into this game for awhile and then stop playing for a year or so but I always come back. The best part about this game is that when it goes on sale it is 10000000% worth the price because it's super cheap for one, but you also get a ridiculous amount of value for the amount of fun you have. You will run into bosses at the worst possible time, you will get hit with multiple crits and lose a hero before you can heal them, you'll forget to change a skill out or forget to bring certain supplies, etc. The key to this game is patience and not getting too upset about things not going your way. Darkest Dungeon is a roguelike, side-scrolling dungeon crawler which tries and successfully makes suffering fun. 

Picture this, a turnbased RPG in which your party of four has a random encounter with some spiders, pretty typical right? Well imagine that the spiders go first, they instantly posion your healer and kill them, they then shoot web at your melee guy pushing him to the back of your line meaning you have to waste turns putting him back to the front so he can attack, during all this your other two party members get so stressed that one starts attacking randomly and the other just dies of a heart attack basically ruining the run. That's darkest dungeon and it happens often. 

The fun is overcoming the odds with a rag tag bunch of killers who manage to get out of the dungeon on the overside. The game priorities placements and positioning as the way you set up your team can be life or death. In the down time between dungeon crawls you can build up your little town, go to the pub and upgrade your team (only for them to die next round losing all your upgrades) the fun isn't about getting to the end, it's the balance of trying to build a team that can get there only for them to all freakout because you didn't buy enough torches. 

Simply put if you enjoy going at a snails pace, taking it slow and really looking over the minute details and feeling that immensely satisfying feeling of over coming a difficult dungeon then this game is for you, often regarded as a classic and for good reason, this is a suffering simulator and call me a masochist but I love it.

I suppose at least ME1's level up system was changed to make it feel closer to the other games, so at least there's that. Also the Mako was fixed a bit and given boosters so it's easier to get around. It still sucks to drive it on certain terrain, but at least that was added.

ME3... well the story and gameplay wasn't changed, so if you weren't a fan of the ending of that game, then this version won't change that. Which is a shame since I feel at the very least they could have added more for your squadmates to do in the endgame. That was one of my favorite things about ME2, the fact that your non active party members were still doing something and not sitting back having an "offscreen tea party." I like the weapon system of 3, and how FINALLY you can just choose which weapons you want to carry with you, though I am bummed that there's not an option to carry a heavy weapon. As for the ending, well maybe it would be too much to ask them to try fix that. Though I will say the journey to get to the ending is exhilirating, and there are plenty of awesome moments on the way, it just really is too bad the finale didn't live up to its potential.

All in all there are still two great Mass Effect games in this bundle and I think that makes it worth it. If you already own those games, you're better off playing the old versions, but if not then this bundle is worth it, especially if it's on sale.

There are some annoying bugs that I've ran into which haven't been fixed since release which is incredibly frustrating at times, and the work around is saving consistently. 

It has dark humour, memorable companions, and stylish post-apocalyptic setting to help lower the barrier to entry. I feel as such the game never drags because of the number of possible ways to go about dealing with the situation you're presented.

For anyone who has a genuine curiosity about CRPGs but unsure where to start, Wasteland 3 for me is one of the best entry points available - it's deep enough to showcase the genre’s strengths, yet accessible enough to welcome new players. Keep an eye on this for sure!

No Man's Sky game has plenty to offer - procedurally generated planets (including weather, terrain, etc.), animals, plants, encounters, etc. It even has base building, freighters and expeditions, and settlement management. But it's unfortunately a mile wide and an inch deep. It tries to do everything, but doesn't do any one thing better than any other game. 

From the moment you leave the starting planet, the game is an exercise in tedium and repetition. I spent 60 hours in this game. I continuously wondered what the point of all of it was. I was never challenged. I never felt a sense of danger. I never had epic moments of wonder or of adventure. 

I feel like I could forgive its monotony and incredible grind if either: I felt I was in a universe with other people, or the UI wasn't so damn dreadful. 

The multiplayer aspects of this game are totally unnecessary. I never fought off pirates beside a random person, nor had to group up with someone to take on a difficult mission. The moments I did interact with others, it was passing by someone in the corridor of the Anomaly or looking at their ship as they came to land in the same place.  Think of Destiny's Tower system, but with more steps between NPCs. 

And I've been saving the worst part for last: the UI. It is genuinely one of the worst user interfaces I've ever used in a game. Sure, it has a quest log and a compendium to track your progress, it has inventories, it has customisation to your exosuit or ship or your tools. Even the crafting menus exist. But that's all that can be said positively about the UI. 

There are ZERO shortcuts. Nearly EVERYTHING requires you to hold a key down for a second, and everything has an animation that you cannot skip or speed up. And you do this several thousand times in your playthrough. Landing a ship? Yep, you have to watch the same animation everytime. Teleporting to a settlement? Yep, hold TAB to skip the forced window that comes up telling you what planet you're on. Opening a box? Hold on, before you take what's in the box, you have to first aim way above it because the icon conflicts with switching off a random light in the middle of a barren wasteland, and then you hold a button to complete an arbitrary second-long interaction before the animation starts and you have to remove the random junk from the front of it so you can then persevere through another animation and a mandatory 2 second waiting period. THEN you will be given an item that you will ignore for your entire playthrough. 

And the UI constantly overrides itself. If I pin a quest, stop overriding it just because I entered a different star system and got attacked by pirates that was entirely out of my control. If I pin a quest, stop overriding it just because I'm holding a map that I received as a quest reward from my last quest. If I pin a quest, stop overriding it just because I accidentally complete a random side objective by using my mining laser on an animal that accidentally stepped in front of me. If I already have the items in my inventory when I pick up a quest, PLEASE for the love of god, let me hand it in immediately - I don't want to have to teleport or fly offworld just to give the game time to realise that I have what I need in my inventory. And stop giving me quest rewards like recipes/blueprints that I already unlocked because I couldn't be bothered waiting for the quest NPC to recognise I had the items in my inventory all along.

The UI is INCREDIBLY frustrating. I think I spent 18 of my 60 hours in this game in animations I couldn't skip, interactions I couldn't make instantaneous, and dialogue that I couldn't skip immediately. 

Overall, No Man's Sky is fine. Someone will enjoy it. But for me, it was mediocre at best and frustratingly tedious at worst.

I am a fallout 4 believer to the chagrin of the rest of fallout fans. To be fair, I am biased in the same way i am biased to dark souls 3 over elden ring. This game was my first foray into the series. Between PC and xbox I have nearly 2 thousand hours in this game. In that time I have found I truly do believe it is a better game than the other bethesda titles. 

I know that last sentence has a few people kicking their monitor, but my main defense here is cohesion. Having played and enjoyed fnv, skyrim, fo3, and a little of oblivion, I can confidently say that fallout 4 is the most convincing and cohesive of the titles. 

For example, Fallout 4 pretty obviously says to the player, "The world before the bombs was bad, but people understood that, adapted to it, and on an average basis liked their lives. After the world ended the world got a whole lot worse but people still function the same. They go about their day, and though that day is harder they still generally like life more than the alternative. This world isn't all doom and gloom, its a comedy with a coat of doom and gloom paint over it." The best way I can really show this is that in f04 there isn't a single child skeleton, and when the death of children is eluded to it is with class and taste. Like a sex scene in a movie where the camera pans away and you here giggling. You understand what happened without it being drawn out for you. While in fnv there's more than one school bus filled with child skeletons on a field trip. 

My main point here is that the other games whiplash between goofy post apocalyptic and terrifying reality, while fo4 is comfortable in respecting your intelligence to understand the reality without giving the whiplash involved in showing it to you blatantly. 

I hope this is coherent. I wrote this on like 4 hours of sleep.

Baldur's Gate 3 isn’t just a great RPG—it’s the kind of game that makes most other RPGs feel slightly unfinished afterward.

At its core, it’s a **turn-based, party-based CRPG set in the Dungeons & Dragons universe**, where almost everything is driven by choice: combat, dialogue, exploration, and even failure. The game constantly reacts to what you do in ways that feel genuinely handcrafted rather than scripted. That level of reactivity is a big reason it’s been called one of the best RPGs ever made.

The biggest strength is how much **player freedom and agency** it gives you. You can solve problems through combat, stealth, persuasion, absurd physics, or just creative nonsense the devs somehow accounted for. It feels less like “following a questline” and more like *actually playing a tabletop campaign with a very ambitious DM*.

Combat is turn-based but extremely flexible. Positioning, abilities, environmental interactions, and party synergy all matter, and even fights you “mess up” can turn into memorable chaos instead of just a reload moment.

And then there’s the writing and characters. The companions are a huge highlight—well-voiced, deeply written, and reactive to your decisions in ways that actually change relationships and outcomes. It’s one of those rare games where you end up caring about your party way more than expected.

But it’s not flawless.

The biggest barrier for some players is the **sheer complexity and pacing**. The game is dense. Systems stack on top of systems (spells, status effects, gear interactions, dialogue checks), and it can feel overwhelming if you’re not used to CRPGs or D&D-style rules. Even fans admit it can feel like “homework” managing everything at times.

There’s also the reality that the game is so big that you can easily miss entire storylines or regions without realizing it. That freedom is impressive, but it can also mean uneven pacing depending on how you play.

And while later acts are still strong, some players note occasional performance dips or rougher pacing compared to the near-perfect opening.

Still, none of that really changes the overall picture.

With **overwhelmingly positive Steam reviews (around 96%+ positive across hundreds of thousands of players)**, it’s clear how widely it’s loved and how impactful it’s been.

**Pros:**

* Insane player freedom and reactivity
* Deep, tactical combat with endless creativity
* Incredible writing and memorable companions
* Huge amount of content and replayability
* Choices actually matter in meaningful ways

**Cons:**

* Very steep learning curve (especially for newcomers)
* Can feel overwhelming or slow to manage
* Easy to miss content due to branching structure
* Some pacing/performance issues in later sections

**Verdict:**
A landmark RPG that sets a new standard for choice-driven storytelling and reactive game design. It’s not always simple, but it’s almost always impressive.

If a developer ever reads this, all I want to say is that please do not be discouraged by all of the haters. You have created something really quite special with this game from a variety of angles and you should be proud of what you have achieved. Even though this game has flaws, you did so many things right even from the beginning that deserve to live on in your future works.

Though not every opportunity was taken to create interesting alternate solutions to quests there is more than has probably existed in any previous Bethesda game outside of Morrowind. A great number of the dialogue options seem to illicit different dialogue responses from your companions in particular. This is a level of production totally unprecedented in Fallout or Elder Scrolls. Furthermore, I find each companion to be a genuinely interesting and three-dimensional character with their own backstory, likes, dislikes, etc. Sometimes they even remember your previous dialogue responses. That goes so far to making them feel genuinely realistic and believable and makes them easy to connect with. Furthermore, I find the story to be genuinely beautiful as well. The ending in particular inspired a grand sense of awe in me. On my first playthrough on a previous platform, certain story events synced up so perfectly with some of my own in game choices that it felt uncanny and made some of the more emotional scenes impact me that much harder. Furthermore the faction questlines are another highlight of this game and there isn't a dull one amongst them. As everyone says, a highlight is the Crimson Fleet one. The UC vanguard is my personal favorite. The new Trackers Alliance content was awesome.

The new game plus mode is next level. A truly bold and brave attempt to do something nobody else has done and it's tragic that so many people who have given this game a chance never got to see it. While it is definitely a good thing that the game contains a quite enormous amount of content that you can spend hundreds of hours on a single playthrough easily, you do yourself a disservice by not seeing what they have in store with NG+ and that is all I will say about it.

I don't know why so many other people overlook it so easily, but the clutter in this game along with the environmental storytelling that comes from it is legendary. There's just so many items you can pick up and examine and they're all very beautifully detailed and modeled. It's painstaking attention to detail. It's pretty rare that you will be in a space station that feels exactly like another. Gone are the days of the same prefab assets copy and pasted. Every space where people inhabit feels genuinely lived in and if you pay attention you can learn lots of little details just from looking at the placement of items or things written on whiteboards. Bethesda is only rivaled by From Software in this department. 

The ability to granularly choose your difficulty settings is quite fantastic, in my opinion. I always appreciated certain survival elements from previous titles, but things like only being able to save at a bed were a dealbreaker for me. 

The ship building, while taking some time to get used to is a lot of fun and I personally really enjoy buying a ship and customizing it to fit my needs. You might need a YouTube tutorial though. Simplification would help but once I got the hang of it I learned to love it.

The on foot combat is quite a lot of fun, and the zero-G combat is a highlight. The physics of it feel very realistic with items floating around all over the place. Firearms send you flying backwards when you use them. These moments are rare, but they are some of the best action set pieces in the game. The ship combat is aggressively difficult at times. Only choice is to lower the difficulty sometimes. But when it works it can be quite fun. It does take a lot of time to get used to messing with your power management under pressure, but that can be mitigated by upgrading your ship.

The economy is good. Even being a hoarder and picking up everything of any kind of positive value-to-weight ratio, making credits isn't all that easy starting out and you will have plenty of things to spend money on. All the vendors have good, unique weapons worth upgrading and that will take you many millions of credits. Amassing that level of fortune to buy all of the guns and ships and allies that you want will take a really long time and this is GOOD. I like having things to spend money on! I don't want millions of gold or caps that I can never spend!

The lockpicking minigame is the best ever. It doesn't get old for me. I get excited when I see a locked door or container.

Sadly, the biggest most glaring flaw with this game is the outpost building and planet exploration, the elements inspired by No Man's Sky. I'm sorry to say, but even adding vehicles can't fix it. Especially due to inventory limits and the resources weighing such an incredible amount, trying to work out the logistics of making the base building happen smoothly is frankly a massive chore. Exploring the barren and boring planets to scan creatures that are super bullet spongey but also want you dead, wasting precious ammo, and just begging, pleading, hoping you will find that last rock or plant you need... You'll go crazy if you try to genuinely engage with this gameplay loop. I think it is probably better to play Starfield entirely ignoring these elements of the game and simply treating it as Fallout 3 in space. Stick to the quests, combat, dialogue, etc. That's where the game shines.

Overall, I wholeheartedly recommend this game. It is truly underrated in my opinion and it truly makes me feel sad that it doesn't have a more positive reception in general. I would absolutely love to see a Starfield 2 someday.

This is the first in a new game series for BGS, so I am pleased with their initial offering, one that will get better in time from future updates.  

My experience was buying the premium edition to play it prior to launch day, I found it fun and promising, despite limitations from few Points of Interests and obvious restrictions from features not implemented for this genre of game. I stopped playing this game after 80-90 hours of play, due to real life taking up game time.

Now that BGS added further content, this game feels fuller, and a broader galaxy. There is more to do, and the POI's seem diverse enough to hold interest through a session of play. The added features filled in some cracks, and lessened my gripes to acceptable degrees.

Some of the gripes I have aren't related to the game but the logic of the game systems, such as searching for water while on an icy planet, only registering in a hard-to-find spring despite ice ubiquity; or, going to a seemingly unexplored planet and finding development across the planet due to the planetary surface auto-generative nature of the game. Still, little things like this are unlikely to ruin the gameplay experience. Some weapon designs are funny looking, as are the fashion designs.

I would say to find out for yourself, this game offers great value in dollars to gameplay hours.

It scratches an itch. Bannerlord have a style of game that could be the sweet spot between Civ style world/kingdom building with a mix of Total War battles. However the execution is verging on poor. 

Vanilla game is okay, its not great. If you want to have any kind of fun then you will absolutely need mods as the base systems and features just arent there. Mods for diplomacy, larger battles and armies are a must.

The positives are; 
- you can play the game multiple different ways (Merc, Trader, Vassel, Ruler) and its completely open as to how you want your character to play out, it doesnt force you into a specific type. 
- The world, for the most part, moves pretty consistantly and things constantly change, kingdoms lose towns and castles and armies declare war on you out of the blue.  
- Battles can be fun and do require some thinking, especially if you find yourself outnumbered. 
- Seiges are a great feature, you just lack the ability to control them well.
- The kingdoms are well thought out and styled and the database that is there could very easily be expanded upon and made to be more interactive.

Cons are; 
- Dialouges are rough and uninteresting, every NPC interaction is identical and repetitive. 
- AI lords and leaders are terrible when it comes to tactics, both in seiges and in battles.
- Wars are persistent and sometimes seem pointlessly invoked and when this happens continuously as you are trying to rebuild or work on other things it came become incredibly frustrating. 
- Graphics are very poor. 
- There is so much potential in the towns and villages if they were more interactive.
- Hideouts are bland and monotonous. 

Overall the potential was huge, but its a basic rendition and for a while it is fun. I would recommend simply for the joy of the first playthrough, after that the cracks in the game start to spoil the overall enjoyment. Buy on discount

Only a few months ago, I would have given Phasmophobia one of the highest ratings possible. It was genuinely one of the most unique games I had ever played. Every investigation felt different, and no two matches were ever exactly the same. It perfectly blended detective work and horror in a way that few games have managed to replicate. For a long time, I proudly called it my favorite game.

I've been playing since the early days, and most updates brought exciting additions that kept the experience fresh. I made countless great memories playing with friends, and it always felt like the developers were building on something special.

Unfortunately, this most recent update has completely changed my opinion.

What was once a polished and engaging experience has become a frustrating, bug-ridden mess. Many of the changes feel unnecessary and actively make the game less enjoyable. The result is a version of Phasmophobia that is simply not fun to play anymore.

The technical issues alone are unacceptable. I've personally encountered numerous bugs, including the Spirit Box—a core piece of evidence—not functioning correctly, settings refusing to save between sessions, clipping through maps, frequent crashes, and even being killed by a ghost after I was already dead. These aren't minor inconveniences; they're game-breaking problems that directly impact the core gameplay experience.

What's even more disappointing is the apparent lack of urgency from the developers. Players have spent years supporting this game, helping it grow from an indie success story into one of the most recognizable multiplayer horror titles on the market. That loyalty deserves to be respected. Instead, many longtime fans feel ignored while the game suffers from issues that should never have made it into a major update.

What makes this situation especially frustrating is that Phasmophobia had everything going for it: a unique concept, a passionate community, tremendous popularity, and the resources to continue improving. Rather than building on those strengths, this update feels like a step backward in nearly every way.

I've rarely seen a game I loved so much decline so quickly. It went from being my favorite game to one of my biggest gaming disappointments. If the developers truly value the community that helped make this game successful, they need to listen to player feedback and seriously reconsider the direction of this update. Otherwise, many longtime players—including myself—may have little reason to return.

I started playing this year and I've been having a lot of fun with the game.

That said, I don't think it's sustainable to keep both 5v5 and 6v6 queues at the same time. The only difference between the two modes is the number of players. If 5v5 was introduced partly to reduce queue times, splitting the player base between two formats just brings back the same issue.

I also understand why many people dislike playing tank in 5v5. Without another tank to share responsibilities, the role is under a lot more pressure and often gets blamed whenever the team loses.

In my opinion, Overwatch should settle on one definitive format and stick with it for both Casual and Competitive. A larger, unified player base would lead to faster queues, more varied matches, and better matchmaking for everyone.

I genuinely loved this game and have already recommended it to friends. Matches are short enough that I can fit them into my daily routine without feeling like I have to sacrifice other responsibilities. I can enjoy the game without needing to dedicate entire evenings to it.

Honestly, I can see myself playing Overwatch for many years to come.
